title: Chapter 3: Methodology
author: Karylle Vinces J. Aliswag & Juana Mari A. Del Rosario

blocks.text: Chapter Three
METHODOLOGY

This chapter presents the research design, the dataset and its sampling, the evaluation metrics and statistical treatment, the proposed Enhanced Seeded Region Growing (ESRG) algorithm and its system architecture, the hardware and software requirements, and the theories, methods, and tools that implement each objective.
3.1 Research Design

This study employs a quantitative, experimental, and applied research design. Quantitative research tests objective theories by examining relationships among measurable variables, and experimental research determines whether a treatment influences an outcome by comparing a treatment group with a control group (Creswell & Creswell, 2023). The study is applied because it addresses the practical need for consistent, automated, and interpretable localization and delineation of brain tumors on two-dimensional (2D) contrast-enhanced T1-weighted (T1-CE) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) slices.

The control group is the original Seeded Region Growing (SRG) algorithm of Adams and Bischof (1994), and the experimental group is the ESRG. The independent variables are the three enhancements: automatic seed selection (Objective 1), the local difference measure computed in the log domain (Objective 2), and the adaptive stopping criterion (Objective 3). The dependent variables are the segmentation-quality metrics of Section 3.1.2.

Both algorithms are run under identical conditions: the same slices, the same seeds, the same parameter values for every applied method, and the same evaluation procedure. The baseline SRG is implemented as published: each candidate pixel is compared with the mean intensity of the adjacent region, the immediate neighbors of a pixel are its 8-connected neighbors (Adams & Bischof, 1994, Section II), and every pixel is absorbed until the whole image has been allocated. Because the original algorithm stops a region only where a competing region reaches a pixel first, it is given competing seeds. The ESRG grows from the tumor seed alone, inside the brain, under the stopping rules of Section 3.4.3.

Seeding is treated as a controlled condition. Under automatic seeding, the tumor seed is selected by the system (Objective 1). Under planted seeding, a simulated careful operator places one seed of each type: a tumor seed at the deepest pixel of the ground-truth tumor core (placement P1), a healthy-tissue seed in the opposite hemisphere at least 25 mm from the tumor core, and a background seed in the air at least 8 pixels outside the brain, each a disk of radius 3 pixels. Two further placements, P2 and P3, move every seed by 4 to 8 mm within its own region, so that the dependence of a result on the exact click position can be measured. The ground-truth mask is used only to position the simulated seeds; the automatic seed never sees it.

The applied methods are switched on and off one at a time from the same seeds. When an enhancement is applied to the SRG baseline, it acts on the tumor region only and uses exactly the parameter values of the ESRG, so the SRG receives no separate tuning. The configurations that result are named and explained with the experiments in Section 3.1.2.
3.1.1 Dataset

The study uses the adult glioma (GLI) and meningioma (MEN) collections of the Brain Tumor Segmentation (BraTS) 2023 challenge (Baid et al., 2021; Bakas et al., 2017; LaBella et al., 2023; Menze et al., 2015). Each case provides co-registered, skull-stripped multiparametric MRI volumes at an isotropic resolution of 1 mm with expert ground-truth labels. Only the post-contrast T1-weighted (T1-CE) volume is used, because contrast enhancement delineates the active tumor. The reference standard is the tumor core, the union of labels 1 (necrotic and non-enhancing tumor core) and 3 (enhancing tumor); the peritumoral edema (label 2) is excluded because it is not visible as tumor on T1-CE images.

For each patient, one axial slice was exported as a PNG image of at most 512 × 512 pixels together with its tumor-core mask, so that one pixel corresponds to 240/512 ≈ 0.469 mm. A slice was eligible if its tumor core covered at least 150 pixels on the native 240-pixel grid (about 150 mm²), and the exported slice was chosen at random among the eligible slices, so that the largest, easiest section is not selected systematically. Intensities are rescaled to 0–255 between the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles, and the brain mask is the non-zero region that skull stripping leaves. These steps belong to the data, not to the algorithm. Every patient contributes exactly one slice, so the slices are independent observations and the unit of analysis is the patient.
Sampling

The evaluated sample was drawn by stratified simple random sampling. The test set, the locked 70% of the pool (Table 3.1), is divided into two strata, glioma and meningioma, and an equal number of patients is drawn at random, without replacement, from each stratum with the fixed random seed 2026. Stratification guarantees that both tumor types are represented, and equal allocation estimates both with the same precision. The drawn list was recorded before the evaluation started.

**Cochran’s sample size formula** (Cochran, 1977) gives the number of patients needed to estimate a proportion, here the seed hit rate of Objective 1, within a chosen margin of error at 95% confidence. Its purpose is to justify the sample size statistically. A smaller margin of error requires a larger sample, and p = 0.5 is the most conservative assumption because it gives the largest sample.

blocks.title: Sample Size Formula for an Unlimited Population

blocks.text: where *n*_{0} is the sample size for an unlimited population, *z* is the standard normal value for 95% confidence, 1.96, *p* is the expected proportion, 0.5, and *e* is the margin of error, 0.05.

**The finite population correction** reduces the required sample when the pool is limited. Its purpose is to avoid sampling more patients than the pool warrants. The smaller the pool, the larger the reduction.
where *n* is the minimum sample size of the tumor type, and *N* is the number of patients of that tumor type in the pool.

The pool, not the test set, is the population to which the results are generalized; because the test set is a random 70% of the pool, a random sample of the test set is a random sample of the pool. With e = 0.05, the first equation gives n_{0} = 384.15, and the second gives a minimum of 276 glioma patients (N = 966) and 256 meningioma patients (N = 759). The larger requirement, 276, was applied to both strata and increased by about 9% as an allowance for cases that cannot be evaluated (Cochran, 1977), giving n_{h} = 300 patients per tumor type and 600 in total. The resulting margins of error at 95% confidence are ±4.7 percentage points for glioma and ±4.4 for meningioma.
Dataset Presented

Table 3.1 presents the dataset. The pool was split once at the patient level, separately for each tumor type and with the fixed random seed 2026, into a development set (30%) and a test set (70%). All parameter tuning used the development set only. The test set was locked until the final configuration had been frozen, and the sample drawn from it was evaluated once; the full record of tuning decisions is kept in the study protocol.

blocks.text: 3.1.2 Evaluation Metrics

Each predicted tumor mask M is compared with the expert ground-truth tumor-core mask G at the working resolution of the slice. Each objective is judged by the metric that responds most directly to its problem (Maier-Hein et al., 2024; Taha & Hanbury, 2015): the seed hit rate for Objective 1, recall for undersegmentation (Objective 2), and precision and HD95 for boundary leakage (Objective 3). The Dice similarity coefficient is the overall measure, and the processing time per slice measures efficiency. The overlap metrics are computed from three pixel counts: the true positives (TP), tumor in both M and G; the false positives (FP), tumor only in M; and the false negatives (FN), tumor only in G.

**Seed Hit Rate (SHR)** is the percentage of slices on which the entire automatic seed lies inside the tumor core. It measures how reliably automatic seed selection starts growth inside the tumor. A higher value is better; a slice on which no seed is found counts as a miss. The target of Objective 1 is a lower confidence bound of at least 70%.
where *n*_{hit} is the number of slices whose seed core lies entirely inside the tumor core, and *n* is the number of slices evaluated.

**Recall** is the share of the true tumor that the segmentation recovers. It measures undersegmentation (Objective 2). A higher value is better: a value of 1 means no tumor was missed, and a low value means part of the tumor was left out.
where TP is the number of tumor pixels found by the segmentation, and FN is the number of tumor pixels the segmentation missed.

**Precision** is the share of the segmented region that is truly tumor. It measures boundary leakage (Objective 3). A higher value is better: a value of 1 means no non-tumor tissue was included, and a low value means the region leaked into the surrounding tissue.
where TP is the number of tumor pixels found by the segmentation, and FP is the number of non-tumor pixels included in the segmentation.

**Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC)** measures the overall overlap between the segmentation and the ground truth. It rewards a method only when both undersegmentation and leakage are controlled, so it serves as the overall measure and as a no-harm check, which confirms that an improvement in one error was not obtained by a larger error of the other type. Values range from 0 (no overlap) to 1 (perfect overlap); a higher value is better, and 0.70 or above is conventionally regarded as good agreement (Zijdenbos et al., 1994).
where TP, FP, and FN are the pixel counts defined above.

**HD95**, the 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance, measures how far the boundary of the segmentation lies from the true tumor boundary. A lower value is better, and a leak produces a high value because it creates boundary pixels far from the true edge. It is computed separately for every slice: the distance from each boundary pixel of one mask to the nearest boundary pixel of the other mask is measured in both directions (Huttenlocher et al., 1993), the distances are combined into one list, and HD95 is the 95th percentile of that list. It is therefore one percentile of one list per slice, not a mean. The largest distance (the classical Hausdorff distance) can be set by a single stray pixel, whereas the 95th percentile ignores the most extreme 5% of the distances. HD95 is given in pixels (1 pixel = 0.469 mm); an empty segmentation receives the image diagonal, the worst possible distance (Maier-Hein et al., 2024).

where ∂M and ∂G are the boundary pixels of the segmentation and of the ground truth, d(p, ∂G) is the Euclidean distance from pixel p to the nearest pixel of ∂G, and *P*_{95} is the 95th percentile of the list D.

**Processing Time** is the time the system needs to segment one slice, from the start of the run to the finished mask, without the scoring against the ground truth. It measures computational efficiency. A lower value is better. Because the batch evaluation runs several slices in parallel on one laptop, the times indicate the relative speed of the configurations, not their absolute speed.
where *t* is the processing time of one slice, in seconds, and *t*_{start} and *t*_{end} are the clock readings at the start and at the end of the segmentation.
Statistical Treatment

Results are reported separately for glioma and meningioma, because the two tumor types differ markedly in how they enhance. Because per-slice DSC values are bounded and often skewed, each configuration is described by its median and interquartile range together with its mean and standard deviation. Every configuration was run on the same slices, so configurations are compared with paired tests. Differences are oriented so that a positive value favors the enhanced configuration; for HD95 and processing time, where lower is better, the sign is reversed. All tests are two-sided at α = .05.

**The Shapiro–Wilk test** (Shapiro & Wilk, 1965) checks whether the paired differences are normally distributed. A p value below .05 means they are not, which justifies the rank-based tests below instead of a paired t-test.

**The Wilcoxon signed-rank test** (Wilcoxon, 1945) compares two paired configurations from the ranks of their per-slice differences. A p value below .05 indicates a systematic difference, and the sign of the median difference shows which configuration is better. Because a negligible difference can reach significance with many slices, the effect size r is also reported. A value of |r| near .1, .3, and .5 indicates a small, medium, and large effect (Fritz et al., 2012); a positive r favors the enhanced configuration.
where *Z* is the standardized Wilcoxon statistic, and *N* is the number of paired slices.

**The Friedman test** (Friedman, 1937) compares more than two related configurations on the same slices, namely the four configurations of E1 and the automatic and planted placements of E2. Each slice ranks the configurations, and a p value below .05 means at least one configuration differs from the others; pairwise Wilcoxon tests then show which.
where *N* is the number of slices, *k* is the number of configurations, and *R*_{j} is the sum of the ranks of configuration j over all slices.

**Kendall’s W** (Kendall & Babington Smith, 1939) expresses the Friedman result as an effect size from 0 to 1. A value near 0 means the ranking changes from slice to slice, so there is no consistent difference; a value near 1 means the configurations are ordered the same way on almost every slice.
where χ_{F}^{2} is the Friedman statistic, and *N* and *k* are the number of slices and of configurations.

**The Wilson score interval** (Wilson, 1927) gives the 95% confidence interval of the seed hit rate. It remains accurate for proportions near 0% and 100%, and it narrows as more slices are evaluated. Objective 1 requires its lower bound to be at least 70%.
where p̂ is the observed proportion of hits, *n* is the number of slices, and *z* is 1.96 for 95% confidence.

**The Holm adjustment** (Holm, 1979) corrects the p values when several tests are made in one experiment, for example for recall and DSC, so that the chance of a false positive across all of them stays at 5%. A result counts as significant only if its adjusted p value is below .05.
where *m* is the number of tests in the experiment, and *p*_{(j)} is the j-th smallest p value of the experiment.

The decision rules were fixed before the test set was evaluated and are applied separately to each tumor type. An effect counts only if its adjusted p value is below .05 and |r| ≥ 0.1. The overall improvement is established if the DSC of both A_ESRG and P_ESRG is significantly higher than that of P_SRG. Objective 1 is met if the lower bound of the Wilson interval of the seed hit rate is at least 70%, the automatic result is identical across repeated runs while the planted results differ across placements, and the automatic DSC is not significantly lower than that of any planted placement. Objective 2 is met if recall is significantly higher and DSC not significantly lower in both E3 and E4. Objective 3 is met if precision is significantly higher, HD95 significantly lower, and DSC not significantly lower in both E5a and E6.

blocks.text: 3.2 Proposed Algorithm and System Architecture
This section presents the ESRG as the modification of the SRG by the three enhancements, and describes how the procedure is organized into an Input–Process–Output system.
3.2.1 Enhanced Seeded Region Growing Algorithm

The ESRG procedure is given below in general form. It keeps the growing loop of the SRG, in which the pixels adjacent to the region are held in a list sorted by their difference measure and the most similar pixel is examined first (Adams & Bischof, 1994), and it replaces or extends that loop with the steps enclosed in a box, each of which implements the objective indicated. The specific algorithm of each step is given under the corresponding objective in Section 3.4, and the parameter values are listed in Table 3.3.
START
Input: an MRI slice and, optionally, seed clicks. Output: the tumor region A.

items.text: 1. Select the seed S automatically from the slice; if the user supplies seeds, use them as S.
2. Express the intensity of every pixel in the log domain.

blocks.text: 3. Set the region A = S. Repeat the following growing pass until no pixel is added to A:

items.text: a. Set the acceptance bounds from the intensity variability of A: the local bound T_{L} and the global bound T_{G}.
b. For each pixel x adjacent to A, compute its local log-domain difference measure δ(x) and insert x into the sequentially sorted list (SSL) in ascending order of δ.

blocks.text: c. While the SSL is not empty, remove the pixel y with the smallest δ:

items.text: i. If δ(y) > T_{L}, end the pass.
ii. If the log intensity of y differs from the running mean m_{A} of A by more than T_{G}, reject y and take the next pixel.

blocks.text: iii. Otherwise, add y to A, update the statistics of A, and insert the neighbors of y into the SSL.

items.text: 4. If A covers more than a fraction φ of the brain, tighten the bounds and regrow from S.

blocks.text: 5. Output A as the tumor region.
END

When manual seeding is selected in the interface, Step 1 is replaced by the user’s clicks, so that the ESRG and the SRG start from identical seeds. The symbols of the procedure are defined with the equations of Section 3.4. The original SRG corresponds to the same loop without the boxed steps, with the difference measured against the mean of the whole region and with every pixel eventually absorbed.

3.2.2 Proposed System Architecture

blocks.title: Input–Process–Output Structure of the Proposed System
blocks.note: The ground-truth mask enters only the Evaluation stage; it is never used during segmentation.

blocks.text: Figure 3.1 presents the architecture of the system in the Input–Process–Output (IPO) model. The Input is a skull-stripped, axial, contrast-enhanced T1-weighted 2D MRI slice stored as a PNG file.

The Process has two parts. In Pre-processing, the Log-Domain Transformation converts the pixel intensities to the log domain and estimates the noise floor, the smallest region variability that the image noise allows. Core Processing then contains the three enhancements: Automatic Seed Selection, which finds the tumor seed through multi-level Otsu thresholding, ranking of the candidates, and a seed core (Objective 1); Region Growing, which compares each pixel with its newly absorbed neighbors in the log domain (Objective 2); and the Adaptive Stopping Criterion, which bounds the growth with the region mean, the σ cap, and the flood guard (Objective 3).

The Output is the enhanced segmentation of the tumor mass, a binary mask that is displayed as an overlay on the slice. Before the mask is returned, its holes are filled, a one-pixel opening removes thin protrusions, and only the part connected to the seed is kept; these clean-up steps are not part of the enhancements. When no candidate survives seed selection, the system reports that no tumor candidate was found instead of placing an arbitrary seed.
The Evaluation compares the output with the ground-truth tumor-core mask using the Dice similarity coefficient, precision, recall, HD95, and the seed hit rate defined in Section 3.1.2.

Install Python 3.10 or later from python.org, including the Tcl/Tk component, and add Python to the system PATH.
Copy the project folder to the computer and open a terminal in that folder.
Optionally, create and activate a virtual environment: python -m venv .venv, then .venv\Scripts\activate on Windows or source .venv/bin/activate on macOS and Linux.
Install the dependencies: pip install -r requirements.txt.
Verify the installation by running the test suite: python tests/test_pipeline.py.
Launch the interface with python -m gui.app, open an MRI slice, choose the method (ESRG or SRG) and the seeding mode (automatic or manual), and press RUN.

To reproduce the study, run in order: python -P experiments/sampling.py --brats --draw (patient-level split), python -P experiments/tune.py --stage all (tuning on the development set), and python -P experiments/evaluate.py --set test --sample-per-type 300 --approved --analyze (the single test run and its analysis).
3.4 Theories, Methods, and Tools

This section presents, for each objective, the theories that justify the enhancement, the methods and algorithms that implement it, and the tools used. The original SRG accepts an intensity image and a set of seeds and grows the seeded regions until all pixels are assimilated (Mehnert & Jackway, 1997), comparing each candidate pixel with the mean intensity of the adjacent region (Adams & Bischof, 1994); the enhancements change how the seed is obtained, what the comparison measures, and when a pixel is absorbed or rejected.
3.4.1 To provide an automatic seed selection option through Multi-Level Otsu Thresholding with connected-component filtering
Theories
Optimal Histogram Thresholding

Otsu’s method separates an image into classes by intensity without operator input (Otsu, 1979). It chooses the thresholds that maximize the between-class variance of the gray-level histogram, which is equivalent to minimizing the variance inside each class. The multi-level extension divides the histogram into K classes with K − 1 thresholds, found efficiently by the recursive search of Liao et al. (2001). A larger between-class variance means the classes are better separated. On T1-CE images the enhancing tumor is among the brightest tissues, so it falls in the highest class.

where *t*_{1}, …, *t*_{K−1} are the thresholds, with *t*_{K−1} separating the highest-intensity class, *ω*_{k} and *μ*_{k} are the pixel fraction and mean intensity of class k, and *μ*_{T} is the mean intensity of all pixels.
Connected Components and Object Interiority

A binary mask can be divided into connected components, groups of foreground pixels linked through their neighbors, so that each candidate structure can be measured and accepted or rejected on its own (Gonzalez & Woods, 2018). The Euclidean distance transform gives each pixel its distance to the nearest pixel outside the component; its maximum lies at the center of the largest inscribed disk, a point that always lies inside the component, even for a ring-enhancing tumor, and avoids boundary pixels affected by the partial volume effect (Tohka, 2014).
Local Contrast of Enhancing Lesions

An enhancing lesion is brighter than its surroundings, which is the principle of the white top-hat transform (Soille, 2003). Automatic seeding from the brightest regions of brain MRI has been used for tumor segmentation on BraTS data (Biratu et al., 2021). Candidates are therefore ranked by their contrast against a surrounding ring, not by absolute brightness alone.
Methods
Automated Seed Selection

Multi-level Otsu thresholding with K = 4 is applied to the interior of the brain, the pixels whose depth from the brain outline exceeds both the minimum clearance c and a fraction η = 0.06 of the maximum depth. The candidate mask keeps the interior pixels of the highest class, and connected-component filtering separates the tumor from other bright structures. Components smaller than A_{min} = 40 pixels are discarded as noise. The remaining components are tested for interiority with the clearance of the following equation, which measures how far the component lies inside the brain beyond its own radius. A larger clearance means a more interior component, and a component is discarded if its clearance is below c. The tuned value is c = 0, because on skull-stripped data no scalp tissue touches the brain outline, while meningiomas, which arise from the meninges, commonly do.

where *x*_{i}^{*} is the pixel of component i farthest from its boundary, depth(*x*_{i}^{*}) is the distance of that pixel from the brain outline, *ρ*_{i} is the inscribed radius of component i, its largest distance-transform value, and *κ*_{i} is the clearance of component i.

The surviving components are ranked by their local contrast Δ_{i}, the mean intensity of the component minus that of a surrounding ring of 6 pixels; their inscribed radius ρ_{i}; and a shape score s_{i} between 0 and 1 that averages compactness and solidity (Gonzalez & Woods, 2018). The ranking score is the weighted sum below, after contrast and radius are rescaled to [0, 1]; a higher score marks a better candidate, and the highest-ranked component is selected. The weights make interiority the dominant criterion, contrast secondary, and shape a tie-breaker. The seed core S is formed from the medial pixels of the selected component, those whose distance-transform value is at least α = 0.85 of its maximum.

where *Q*_{i} is the ranking score of component i, *Δ*_{i}′ and *ρ*_{i}′ are the rescaled contrast and inscribed radius, *s*_{i} is the shape score, and *w*_{c}, *w*_{r}, and *w*_{s} are the weights 0.5, 1, and 0.2.

Seed selection remains optional: in manual mode each click is dilated into a disk of radius 3 pixels and used as it is, and the SRG additionally accepts clicks for its competing healthy-tissue and background regions. Under automatic seeding, the SRG uses the same automatic tumor seed with planted competing seeds. The seed-selection parameters were tuned on the development set by the seed hit rate, which does not depend on the growth rule.
Algorithm of Automated Seed Selection
START
Input: the normalized brain-masked slice, the brain mask and its depth map, and the parameters of Table 3.3. Output: the seed core S, or “no tumor candidate.”
1. Form the interior region of the brain; if it is empty or has constant intensity, return “no tumor candidate.”
2. Compute the K − 1 multi-level Otsu thresholds of the interior region.
3. Form the candidate mask from the interior pixels of the highest class, open it, and label its components; if there are none, return “no tumor candidate.”
4. Discard each component whose area is below A_{min} or whose clearance is below c; if none remains, return “no tumor candidate.”
5. For each remaining component, compute its contrast, inscribed radius, and shape score, rescale contrast and radius, and compute its ranking score.
6. Select the component with the highest ranking score, form S from its medial pixels, and output S.
END
Tools

Image loading and resizing use Pillow (Clark, 2015); percentile normalization uses NumPy (Harris et al., 2020). The Otsu and multi-level Otsu thresholds, disk structuring elements, morphological opening, and the region properties of the shape score come from scikit-image (van der Walt et al., 2014). Connected-component labeling and the Euclidean distance transform come from SciPy’s ndimage module (Virtanen et al., 2020). The Tkinter interface captures the clicks of the manual seeding option.
3.4.2 To minimize undersegmentation by replacing the global-mean difference with a local difference measure computed in the log domain, making the criterion insensitive to multiplicative bias
Theories
The Global Homogeneity Assumption of the Original Difference Measure

The original SRG compares each candidate pixel with the mean intensity of the entire adjacent region (Adams & Bischof, 1994). A single region mean represents every pixel of the region only if the region is intensity-homogeneous. Brain tumors violate this assumption: tumor tissue is often heterogeneous, and the scanner superimposes a smooth intensity inhomogeneity on the image (Li et al., 2011). Pixels of the same tumor that lie far from the seed can then differ from the region mean more than they differ from their neighbors, so part of the tumor is left unsegmented (Akram et al., 2017).
The Multiplicative Bias-Field Model

Intensity inhomogeneity is modeled as a smooth, positive bias field that multiplies the true tissue signal (Li et al., 2011). The logarithm turns the multiplication into an addition, which is also the domain in which N4ITK models the field (Tustison et al., 2010). The model is not a result to be interpreted; it explains why the log domain is useful.

blocks.title: Bias-Field Model in the Log Domain

blocks.text: where *I*(*x*) is the observed intensity of pixel x, *J*(*x*) is the true tissue signal, and *b*(*x*) is the bias field, which varies slowly across the image.

Because the bias field varies slowly, it is nearly the same for two neighboring pixels, so it cancels when their log intensities are subtracted. The difference between a pixel and its neighbors in the log domain therefore reflects the tissue, not the bias.

blocks.title: Cancellation of the Bias Field Between Neighboring Pixels

blocks.text: where *L*(*x*) and *L*(*y*) are the log-domain intensities of pixels x and y, and *W*_{r}(*x*) is the small window of radius r around x, within which the bias field is nearly constant.
Methods
Log-Domain Transformation

Every pixel of the normalized, brain-masked slice is transformed with the following equation. Its purpose is to make the multiplicative bias additive so that nearby pixels can be compared. A higher value of L means a brighter pixel; the offset ε prevents the logarithm of zero and has no practical effect on tissue intensities.
where *L*(*x*) is the log-domain intensity of pixel x, *I*(*x*) is the normalized intensity from 0 to 255, equal to 0 outside the brain, and *ε* is an offset of 1.

The log-domain image is also used to estimate the noise floor σ_{floor}, the smallest region standard deviation that the image noise allows, which the stopping criterion uses as a lower bound. It is 1.4826 times the median absolute deviation of the difference between L and its 3 × 3 median within the brain, a robust estimate of the noise that ignores the large differences at tissue edges (Donoho & Johnstone, 1994; Leys et al., 2013; Rousseeuw & Croux, 1993), bounded below by 0.02 log units.
Local Log-Domain Difference Measure

The original SRG measures how different a candidate pixel is from the adjacent region with the following equation (Adams & Bischof, 1994). Its purpose is to order the candidates: the smaller the value, the more similar the pixel is to the region and the earlier it is absorbed.

blocks.title: Difference Measure of the Original SRG

blocks.text: where *δ*_{SRG}(*x*) is the difference measure of candidate x, *g*(*x*) is the normalized intensity of x, and *A* is the region adjacent to x.

Because the reference is the mean of the whole region, tumor pixels in a darker part of a heterogeneous tumor, or on the darker side of a bias gradient, differ from it even though they belong to the tumor. The enhanced measure instead compares x, in the log domain, with the mean log intensity of only those region pixels inside a small window around x, that is, with the pixels most recently absorbed next to it. As before, a smaller value means a more similar pixel. With r = 1 the window is 3 × 3 pixels, so each candidate is compared with the absorbed pixels that touch it, and by the cancellation above the bias field does not affect the comparison.

where *δ*(*x*) is the local log-domain difference measure of candidate x, *W*_{r}(*x*) is the (2r + 1) × (2r + 1) window centered on x, *A* ∩ *W*_{r}(*x*) is the set of region pixels inside that window, and *μ*_{loc}(*x*) is their mean log intensity.
Algorithm of the Local Log-Domain Difference Measure
START
Input: the log-domain image L, the current region A, a candidate pixel x, and the window radius r. Output: δ(x).
1. Define the window of radius r centered on x, clipped at the image border.
2. From the arrays that store L and the membership of every absorbed pixel, sum the log intensities and count the region pixels in the window.
3. Compute the local mean as the sum divided by the count; if the count is zero, use the current region mean.
4. Output δ(x) as the absolute difference between L(x) and the local mean.
END
Tools

The logarithm, absolute differences, and medians are computed with NumPy (Harris et al., 2020), and the 3 × 3 median filter is SciPy’s ndimage.median_filter (Virtanen et al., 2020). The per-pixel arrays that supply the window sums are NumPy arrays updated as each pixel is absorbed.
3.4.3 To decrease boundary leakage by integrating a stopping criterion that adapts to the intensity variability of the growing region, supported with a global drift guard
Theories
Unconditional Absorption in the Original Algorithm

In the SRG, the candidate pixels bordering the region are held in a sequentially sorted list (SSL) ordered by their difference measure, and the most similar candidate is always absorbed first (Adams & Bischof, 1994). The original algorithm absorbs the next candidate unconditionally and stops only when every pixel has been assigned to a region. With a single tumor seed, or where the tumor boundary is weak, nothing prevents the region from crossing the boundary and flooding the surrounding tissue. Because the list is sorted, however, a bound on the difference measure can halt a growing pass exactly: once the candidate at the top of the list fails the bound, every candidate behind it fails as well.
The Rician Noise Model and Statistical Region Membership

The magnitude noise of MR images follows a Rician distribution, which approaches a Gaussian distribution when the signal-to-noise ratio exceeds about two (Gudbjartsson & Patz, 1995). The intensities of a homogeneous region can therefore be modeled as approximately normal about the region mean, so a pixel several standard deviations away is unlikely to belong to the region; even without assuming normality, Chebyshev’s inequality limits the share of values k or more standard deviations from the mean to at most 1/k² (Ross, 2019). This justifies a rule that adapts to the variability of each region, the basis of confidence-connected region growing (Insight Software Consortium, n.d.).
Numerically Stable Running Statistics

The region mean and standard deviation must be updated as pixels are absorbed. Welford’s (1962) one-pass method updates both from each new value without storing the region and without the cancellation error of the sum-of-squares formula.
Methods
Adaptive Stopping Criterion

The running mean m_{A} and standard deviation s_{A} of the log intensity are accumulated with Welford’s method from the seed onward. At the start of each pass, the region standard deviation is read and bounded below by the noise floor and above by σ_{cap}. A larger value of σ_{A} gives wider, more permissive bounds; the floor prevents a nearly uniform seed from producing bounds near zero, and the cap, 0.08 log units, prevents a heterogeneous seed from producing bounds so wide that growth floods the brain.

where *s*_{A} is the running sample standard deviation of the region, *σ*_{floor} is the noise floor, *σ*_{cap} is the upper bound, and *σ*_{A} is the region standard deviation used throughout the pass.

The two acceptance bounds of the pass are multiples of σ_{A}. The local bound limits how different a candidate may be from its neighbors, and the global bound limits how far it may stray from the region mean. A larger multiplier makes the bound more permissive.
where *T*_{L} and *T*_{G} are the local and global bounds, and *k*_{L} and *k*_{G} are the local and global multipliers, 4 and 5.

A candidate y at the top of the list is absorbed only if it satisfies both conditions below. When it fails the local bound, the pass ends, because the list is sorted by δ and every remaining candidate also fails; this is the stopping criterion, and it adapts to the variability of the growing region. When it passes the local bound but fails the global bound, it is rejected and never reconsidered; this global drift guard blocks slow chaining across a soft boundary, where each pixel resembles its neighbor but the region gradually drifts away from the tumor intensity. The global test uses the running mean of the region, so the reference follows the region as it grows. The standard deviation σ_{A} stays frozen during a pass, because updating it after every absorption would let each borderline pixel widen the bounds and admit the next. Growth ends when a pass adds no pixel or after 4 passes.
where *δ*(*y*) is the local log-domain difference measure of candidate y, and *m*_{A} is the running mean of the log intensity of the region when y is examined.
Flood Guard

A bound derived from the region’s own variability fails when the seed statistics are unrepresentative, and the region may then cover most of the brain. The flood guard detects this from the size of the region and repeats the growth with tighter bounds, up to 3 times. Because φ = 0.150 is derived from the sizes of real tumors in the development data and not from the output of any method, the guard is triggered only by regions larger than almost every tumor.

where |*A*| and |*B*| are the areas of the grown region and of the brain, in pixels, *φ* is the flood fraction, 0.150, *λ* is the shrink factor, 0.7, and *t* and *t*_{max} are the retry number and the maximum number of retries, 3.

When the stopping criterion is applied to the baseline SRG, it acts on the tumor region only, with the same multipliers and flood guard; the SRG has no passes, so σ_{A} is read from the running statistics at each decision, and a declined pixel is left to the competing regions. In the configurations without the local measure, where the intensity is not in log units, the upper bound σ_{cap} is omitted.
Algorithm of the Adaptive Stopping Criterion
START
Input: the log-domain image, the brain mask, the seed core S, the noise floor, and the parameters of Table 3.3. Output: the grown tumor region A.
1. Set A = S and add the log intensity of every seed pixel to the running statistics.
2. For each pass, up to the maximum number of passes:
a. Read s_{A}, bound it by the noise floor and the cap to obtain σ_{A}, and set T_{L} and T_{G}.
b. Start an empty SSL and insert every neighbor of A that lies in the brain and is neither in A nor rejected, with its δ.
c. While the SSL is not empty, remove the pixel y with the smallest δ:
i. If y is in A or rejected, skip it.
ii. Recompute δ(y); if it has increased, reinsert y and continue.
iii. If δ(y) > T_{L}, end the pass.
iv. If the log intensity of y differs from m_{A} by more than T_{G}, reject y and continue.
v. Otherwise, add y to A, update m_{A}, s_{A}, and the window arrays, and insert its eligible neighbors into the SSL.
d. If no pixel was added during the pass, exit the loop.
3. If A covers more than a fraction φ of the brain and fewer than t_{max} retries have been made, multiply k_{L} and k_{G} by λ, reset A = S, and return to Step 2.
4. Output A.
END
Tools

The SSL is implemented with Python’s standard-library binary heap, heapq, which retrieves the candidate with the smallest δ in logarithmic time (Python Software Foundation, n.d.). The Welford accumulators, the acceptance tests, and the flood guard are implemented directly in Python (Welford, 1962). Connected-component labeling uses SciPy’s ndimage module (Virtanen et al., 2020).
